"Total distance travelled" counts the journey **up and back down**, so it is twice the
greatest height — not the net displacement, which is zero.
**Step 1 — find when the ball is highest.**
s = 22t − 11t²
ds/dt = 22 − 22t = 0
**t = 1**
**Step 2 — confirm it is a maximum.** d²s/dt² = **−22 < 0** ✓
**Step 3 — find the greatest height.**
s(1) = 22(1) − 11(1)² = 22 − 11 = **11 units**
**Step 4 — find when the ball returns.**
22t − 11t² = 0
11t(2 − t) = 0
**t = 0** (launch) or **t = 2** (landing)
so the flight lasts 2 seconds, symmetric about the peak at t = 1 ✓
**Step 5 — add the two legs.**
distance up = **11**
distance down = **11**
total = **22 units** ✓
**The distinction being tested.** At t = 2 the ball is back where it started, so its
**displacement** is 0 — but it has **travelled** 22 units. Distance adds the magnitudes of
each leg regardless of direction ✓ Option (4), 11 units, is the greatest height, which is
the distance travelled on the way up only.
**Checking with the velocity.** v = ds/dt = 22 − 22t:
at t = 0: v = **+22** (rising)
at t = 1: v = **0** (instantaneously at rest at the top)
at t = 2: v = **−22** (falling at the same speed it was thrown)
The speed is symmetric, so the two legs take equal times and cover equal distances ✓
**Computing it by integration, for confirmation.** The total distance is
∫₀² |v| dt = ∫₀¹(22 − 22t)dt + ∫₁²(22t − 22)dt
= [22t − 11t²]₀¹ + [11t² − 22t]₁²
= 11 + [(44 − 44) − (11 − 22)]
= 11 + 11 = **22** ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **44** ✗ would be four legs, or twice the total; **33** ✗
corresponds to no natural quantity here. The structure — rise 11, fall 11 — makes 22 the
only sensible total.
∴ 22 units.

The sum of **all** the binomial coefficients in a row is a power of 2, so subtract the two
that are missing.
**Step 1 — recall the full sum.** Putting x = 1 in the binomial expansion of (1 + x)¹⁰:
¹⁰C₀ + ¹⁰C₁ + ¹⁰C₂ + ⋯ + ¹⁰C₁₀ = **2¹⁰**
**Step 2 — identify what the question leaves out.** It runs from ¹⁰C₁ to ¹⁰C₉, so the
**first** and **last** terms are excluded:
¹⁰C₀ = **1** and ¹⁰C₁₀ = **1**
**Step 3 — subtract.**
¹⁰C₁ + ¹⁰C₂ + ⋯ + ¹⁰C₉ = 2¹⁰ − 1 − 1
= **2¹⁰ − 2** ✓
**Numerically.** 2¹⁰ = 1024, so the answer is **1022**.
**Check by direct addition.** The row of Pascal's triangle for n = 10 is
1, 10, 45, 120, 210, 252, 210, 120, 45, 10, 1
Dropping the two 1s and adding the rest:
10 + 45 + 120 + 210 + 252 + 210 + 120 + 45 + 10
= (10 + 10) + (45 + 45) + (120 + 120) + (210 + 210) + 252
= 20 + 90 + 240 + 420 + 252
= **1022** ✓
**Why the full sum is 2ⁿ.** Choosing a subset of an n-element set means deciding, for
each element, whether to include it — 2 choices each, so **2ⁿ** subsets in all. Grouping
them by size gives ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + ⋯ + ⁿCₙ = 2ⁿ ✓
**Reading the distractors.**
**2¹⁰ − 1** ✗ removes only **one** of the two end terms — the commonest slip, and the
right answer to the sum from ¹⁰C₁ to ¹⁰C₁₀.
**2¹⁰** ✗ is the complete sum, with neither end removed.
**2¹¹** ✗ is the sum for n = 11.
Counting **which** terms are absent is the whole question: the sum starts at the subscript
**1**, not 0, and stops at **9**, not 10 — so two terms are missing, each equal to 1 ✓
∴ 2¹⁰ − 2.

The last digit of a power repeats in a short **cycle**, so reduce the exponent modulo the
cycle length.
**Step 1 — find the cycle for powers of 7.**
7¹ = **7**
7² = 4**9**
7³ = 34**3**
7⁴ = 240**1**
7⁵ = 1680**7** — the pattern repeats
so the cycle of last digits is **7, 9, 3, 1**, of length **4**.
**Step 2 — reduce the exponent modulo 4.**
886 = 4 × 221 + **2**
(since 4 × 221 = 884.)
**Step 3 — read off the cycle position.** A remainder of **2** points to the **second**
entry of the cycle:
last digit = **9** ✓
**A quick way to find the remainder.** A number is divisible by 4 exactly when its **last
two digits** are. Here 86 ÷ 4 = 21 remainder **2** ✓ — no need to divide 886 itself.
**Confirming with modular arithmetic.** Since 7⁴ = 2401 ≡ **1** (mod 10),
7⁸⁸⁶ = 7^(4×221 + 2) = (7⁴)²²¹ × 7² ≡ 1²²¹ × 49 ≡ **9** (mod 10) ✓
**Care with a remainder of zero.** Had the exponent been a multiple of 4 — say 888 — the
remainder would be 0 and the answer would be the **last** entry of the cycle, **1**, not
the first. Mapping remainder 0 to position 4 is the one place this method trips people up.
**The cycles for the other digits**, worth knowing:
2: 2, 4, 8, 6 (length 4)
3: 3, 9, 7, 1 (length 4)
7: **7, 9, 3, 1** (length 4)
8: 8, 4, 2, 6 (length 4)
4 and 9: length 2; 5 and 6: length 1; 0 and 1: length 1
**Reading the distractors.** Each is an entry of the 7-cycle: **7** for remainder 1,
**3** for remainder 3, **1** for remainder 0. Only remainder **2** gives 9 ✓ so the whole
question reduces to computing 886 mod 4 correctly.
∴ 9.
kcet|Mathematics|2012|46||0|0:
The notation (24, 92) means the **greatest common divisor**, and expressing it as
24m + 92n is **Bézout's identity** — found by running the Euclidean algorithm backwards.
**Step 1 — find the gcd by the Euclidean algorithm.**
92 = 3 × 24 + **20**
24 = 1 × 20 + **4**
20 = 5 × 4 + **0**
so **(24, 92) = 4**
**Step 2 — work backwards to express 4 in terms of 24 and 92.** From the second line:
4 = 24 − 1 × 20
and from the first line, 20 = 92 − 3 × 24, so substituting:
4 = 24 − (92 − 3 × 24)
= 24 − 92 + 3 × 24
= **4 × 24 − 1 × 92**
**Step 3 — read off m and n.**
24m + 92n = 4 with **m = 4** and **n = −1**
so **(m, n) = (4, −1)** ✓
**Check.** 24(4) + 92(−1) = 96 − 92 = **4** ✓ which is indeed the gcd.
**Testing the other options.**
(−4, 3): 24(−4) + 92(3) = −96 + 276 = **180** ✗
(−1, 4): −24 + 368 = **344** ✗
(4, −3): 96 − 276 = **−180** ✗
Only (4, −1) gives 4 ✓ and substituting each pair is the quickest check — one
multiplication and one addition apiece.
**Why one coefficient must be negative.** Both 24 and 92 are **positive** and larger than
4, so a combination equalling 4 cannot have both coefficients positive ✓ That observation
alone eliminates nothing here (all four options have a negative entry), but it is a useful
sanity check in general.
**On uniqueness.** The pair is **not** unique: adding 23 to m and subtracting 6 from n
gives another solution, since 24(23) = 92(6) = 552. The general solution is
m = 4 + 23k, n = −1 − 6k for any integer k ✓ The question offers only one of these, so no
ambiguity arises.
∴ (4, −1).

kcet|Mathematics|2012|50||0|0.s:
A subgroup must be a **subset** of G that is itself a group under the same operation —
so it needs the **identity** and an **inverse** for each of its elements.
**The group.** G = {2ⁿ : n ∈ Z} under multiplication, containing …, 1/4, 1/2, **1**, 2,
4, … — all integer powers of 2, positive and negative.
**Testing {4ⁿ : n ∈ Z}.** ✓ **a subgroup**
**subset?** 4ⁿ = 2^(2n), and 2n is an integer, so yes ✓
**closed?** 4^m × 4ⁿ = 4^(m+n) ✓
**identity?** 4⁰ = **1**, which is in the set ✓
**inverses?** the inverse of 4ⁿ is 4^(−n), and −n ∈ Z ✓
All four conditions hold.
**Testing {4ⁿ : n ∈ N}.** ✗ **not a subgroup**
It is a subset and is closed, but the **inverses fail**: the inverse of 4 is 1/4 = 4⁻¹,
and −1 is not a natural number ✗ So no element except the identity has an inverse inside
the set. (Even if N is taken to include 0, giving the identity, the inverses are still
missing.)
**Testing {3ⁿ : n ∈ Z}.** ✗ — not even a **subset** of G, since 3 is not a power of 2 ✓
A subgroup must live inside the parent group.
**Testing {6ⁿ : n ∈ Z}.** ✗ — likewise 6 is not a power of 2.
**Step — conclude.** Only **{4ⁿ : n ∈ Z}** satisfies all the requirements ✓
**What this subgroup is.** It consists of the **even** powers of 2: …, 1/16, 1/4, 1, 4,
16, … — the elements 2^(2n). It is the image of G under squaring, and it has index 2 in
G, the other coset being the odd powers of 2.
**The general lesson.** When checking a candidate subgroup, the two conditions most often
overlooked are **the identity** and **closure under inverses**. A set indexed by **N**
rather than **Z** almost always fails the second, because negative exponents are what
provide the inverses ✓ That single observation distinguishes the first two options.
∴ {4ⁿ : n ∈ Z}.

Note: the printed key gives the second option, {4ⁿ : n ∈ N}. That set contains no inverse
for 4 — the required 4⁻¹ = 1/4 needs n = −1, which is not a natural number — so it is not
a subgroup. The key has been corrected to the first option, where n ranges over Z.

kcet|Mathematics|2012|51||0|0.s:
Solve 4 ⊗₇ x = 5 by multiplying both sides by the **inverse of 4** modulo 7.
**Step 1 — write the congruence.**
4x ≡ 5 (mod 7)
**Step 2 — find the inverse of 4 modulo 7.** We need y with 4y ≡ 1 (mod 7):
4 × 1 = 4, 4 × **2** = 8 ≡ **1** ✓
so **4⁻¹ = 2**
**Step 3 — multiply both sides by 2.**
2 × 4x ≡ 2 × 5 (mod 7)
8x ≡ 10 (mod 7)
x ≡ **3** (mod 7), since 8 ≡ 1 and 10 ≡ 3
**Step 4 — check 3 is in the group.** G = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} ✓ and
**x = 3** ✓
**Check directly.** 4 ⊗₇ 3 = 12 mod 7 = **5** ✓ as required.
**Testing all the options**, which is quick in a group this small:
4 ⊗₇ 5 = 20 mod 7 = **6** ✗
4 ⊗₇ 3 = 12 mod 7 = **5** ✓
4 ⊗₇ 2 = 8 mod 7 = **1** ✗
4 ⊗₇ 4 = 16 mod 7 = **2** ✗
Only 3 works ✓
**Why the solution is unique.** G = {1, …, 6} under multiplication mod 7 **is** a group —
7 is prime, so every non-zero residue has an inverse ✓ In a group the equation ax = b has
exactly one solution, x = a⁻¹b, so no second answer can exist.
**The inverse table for this group**, worth having:
1⁻¹ = **1**, 2⁻¹ = **4**, 3⁻¹ = **5**, 4⁻¹ = **2**, 5⁻¹ = **3**, 6⁻¹ = **6**
(each pair multiplying to 7k + 1: 2 × 4 = 8, 3 × 5 = 15, 6 × 6 = 36 ✓)
**Why 7 must be prime.** If the modulus had factors — say 6 — then elements like 2 and 3
would multiply to 0 and have no inverses, and {1, …, 5} would not be a group under ⊗₆ at
all. The primality of 7 is what makes the question well posed.
∴ 3.

The condition **|β| = 1** is what makes the modulus collapse: with it, the numerator and
denominator turn out to have the **same** modulus.
**Step 1 — use |β| = 1 in the form ββ̄ = 1.**
**Step 2 — multiply the denominator by β̄**, which has modulus 1 and so does not change
any modulus:
β̄(1 − ᾱβ) = β̄ − ᾱββ̄
= β̄ − ᾱ(1)
= **β̄ − ᾱ**
**Step 3 — recognise what that is.** β̄ − ᾱ is the **conjugate** of β − α, and conjugation
preserves modulus:
|β̄ − ᾱ| = **|β − α|**
**Step 4 — assemble.** Since |β̄| = 1,
|1 − ᾱβ| = |β̄| |1 − ᾱβ| = |β̄(1 − ᾱβ)| = |β̄ − ᾱ| = **|β − α|**
so numerator and denominator have **equal** moduli and
|(β − α)/(1 − ᾱβ)| = **1** ✓
**Check with numbers.** Take **β = i** (modulus 1 ✓) and **α = 2**:
numerator: β − α = **i − 2**, modulus √(4 + 1) = **√5**
denominator: 1 − ᾱβ = 1 − 2i, modulus √(1 + 4) = **√5** ✓
quotient modulus = √5/√5 = **1** ✓
**Another check.** β = (1 + i)/√2 (modulus 1 ✓) and α = 3i:
β − α = 0·7071 + 0·7071i − 3i = 0·7071 − 2·2929i, modulus **2·4**
1 − ᾱβ = 1 − (−3i)(0·7071 + 0·7071i) = 1 + 2·1213i + 2·1213i² = −1·1213 + 2·1213i,
modulus **2·4** ✓ equal again.
**What the map means.** The function z ↦ (z − α)/(1 − ᾱz) is a **Möbius transformation**
that maps the unit disc to itself, carrying the unit **circle** to the unit circle. The
question is precisely the statement that points on the circle stay on the circle ✓
**Why α and β must be different.** If α = β the numerator vanishes and the quotient is 0,
not 1 — the question excludes that case explicitly ✓ (Also, if |α| = 1 and α = β the
denominator would vanish too.)
**Reading the distractors.** The answer is independent of α entirely, which is the
surprise. **2**, **1/2** and **1/3** would each require the two moduli to differ by a
fixed factor, but the calculation shows they are always **equal** ✓
∴ 1.

The determinant of a **power** is the power of the determinant, so take the cube root
first.
**Step 1 — use the multiplicative property.** For any square matrix,
|A³| = |A|³
so
|A|³ = 125
**|A| = 5** (taking the real cube root — 125 has only one.)
**Step 2 — compute |A| from the matrix.** With A = [[α, 2], [2, α]]:
|A| = α·α − 2·2 = **α² − 4**
**Step 3 — solve.**
α² − 4 = 5
α² = 9
**α = ±3** ✓
**Check with α = 3.** A = [[3, 2], [2, 3]], so |A| = 9 − 4 = **5** and |A³| = 5³ =
**125** ✓
**Check with α = −3.** A = [[−3, 2], [2, −3]], so |A| = 9 − 4 = **5** ✓ the same, since
only α² appears.
**Why both signs work.** The determinant α² − 4 depends on α only through **α²**, so α
and −α give the same determinant ✓ The answer must therefore be a ± pair, which is why
all four options are written that way.
**Why the cube root is unique.** Over the reals, x³ = 125 has the single solution x = 5 —
unlike a square root, a cube root introduces no ± ambiguity ✓ So |A| = 5 exactly, and the
± enters only at the final step from α² = 9.
**Testing the other options.**
α = ±1: |A| = 1 − 4 = −3, and (−3)³ = **−27** ✗
α = ±2: |A| = 4 − 4 = 0, and 0³ = **0** ✗ (the matrix would be singular)
α = ±5: |A| = 25 − 4 = 21, and 21³ = **9261** ✗
Only α = ±3 gives 125 ✓ and substituting each candidate into (α² − 4)³ is the quickest
check.
**The property used.** |AB| = |A||B| for square matrices of the same order, and applying
it twice gives |A³| = |A|³ ✓ The same rule gives |Aⁿ| = |A|ⁿ for any positive integer n,
and |A⁻¹| = 1/|A|.
∴ ±3.

kcet|Mathematics|2013|24||0|0.s:
The condition a² = e says that a, multiplied by **itself**, gives the identity — which is
exactly what it means for a to be its own inverse.
**Step 1 — recall the definition of an inverse.** The element a⁻¹ is the unique element
with
a · a⁻¹ = a⁻¹ · a = **e**
**Step 2 — compare with the given condition.**
a² = a · a = **e**
So a satisfies the defining property of a⁻¹ ✓
**Step 3 — invoke uniqueness.** In a group the inverse of an element is **unique**, so
from a · a = e it follows that
**a = a⁻¹** ✓
**Elements satisfying a² = e are called involutions.** The identity itself always
qualifies, since e² = e, but there may be others.
**Examples.**
In (Z₆, ⊕₆): 3 ⊕ 3 = 6 ≡ **0** = e ✓ so **3 is its own inverse**, and 3 ≠ e.
In the group {1, −1} under multiplication: (−1)² = **1** ✓
In the group of 2 × 2 matrices, the reflection [[1, 0], [0, −1]] squares to the identity ✓
**Why a = e is too strong.** Option (4) claims the condition forces a to **be** the
identity, but the examples above show otherwise: 3 in Z₆ satisfies 3² = e yet 3 ≠ e ✓ The
condition says a is **self-inverse**, not that it is trivial.
**Why √e is meaningless.** Option (2) writes a = √e, but a square root is not defined in
a general group — there is no such operation, and in any case the equation a² = e may
have several solutions, so "the" square root would be ambiguous ✓
**Why a = 1/a² is wrong.** Option (3) uses the notation 1/a², which in a group means
(a²)⁻¹ = e⁻¹ = **e**. So the statement reads a = e, which as shown is not forced ✓
**A consequence worth noting.** If **every** element of a group satisfies a² = e, then
the group is **abelian**: from (ab)² = e we get abab = e, and multiplying by a on the
left and b on the right gives ba = ab ✓
∴ a = a⁻¹.

kcet|Mathematics|2013|25||0|0.s:
Find the **identity** of the operation first; the inverse of any element follows at once.
**Step 1 — find the identity e.** It must satisfy a ∗ e = a for every integer a:
a + e − n = a
**e = n**
(and e ∗ a = e + a − n = a ✓ so it works on both sides.)
**Step 2 — find the inverse of a general element x.** It is the y with x ∗ y = e:
x + y − n = n
**y = 2n − x**
**Step 3 — apply it to x = −n.**
inverse of (−n) = 2n − (−n) = 2n + n = **3n** ✓
**Check.** (−n) ∗ 3n = (−n) + 3n − n = **n** = e ✓ and
3n ∗ (−n) = 3n − n − n = **n** = e ✓ both ways.
**Check the identity with a sample.** Take n = 5, so e = 5 and the operation is
a ∗ b = a + b − 5. Then
7 ∗ 5 = 7 + 5 − 5 = **7** ✓ the identity works
and the inverse of −5 should be 15: (−5) ∗ 15 = −5 + 15 − 5 = **5** = e ✓
**Why the identity is n and not 0.** The operation subtracts n every time, so the element
that leaves a unchanged must **add back** that n ✓ Substituting u = a − n turns ∗ into
ordinary addition, and the identity a = n corresponds to u = 0.
**Confirming the group structure.** (Z, ∗) is
**closed** ✓ a + b − n is an integer
**associative** ✓ both bracketings give a + b + c − 2n
**has identity** n ✓
**has inverses** 2n − x, always an integer ✓
so it is a genuine group — in fact isomorphic to (Z, +) by the map a ↦ a − n.
**Reading the distractors.** **n** ✗ is the **identity**, not the inverse of −n — the
commonest confusion. **−n** ✗ is the element itself. **−3n** ✗ has the right magnitude but
the wrong sign: checking, (−n) ∗ (−3n) = −n − 3n − n = −5n ≠ n unless n = 0 ✗
The formula **inverse of x = 2e − x** (here 2n − x) is worth remembering for operations of
this shifted-addition type.
∴ 3n.

kcet|Mathematics|2013|27||0|0.s:
Expand the perpendicularity condition as a **dot product** and use ā ⊥ b̄ to kill the
cross terms.
**Step 1 — write what ā ⊥ b̄ gives.**
**ā · b̄ = 0** (and hence b̄ · ā = 0 as well, since the dot product is symmetric.)
**Step 2 — write the second perpendicularity condition.**
(ā + b̄) · (ā + m b̄) = 0
**Step 3 — expand by distributivity.**
ā·ā + m(ā·b̄) + b̄·ā + m(b̄·b̄) = 0
**Step 4 — substitute ā·b̄ = 0.** The two middle terms vanish:
|ā|² + 0 + 0 + m|b̄|² = 0
**Step 5 — solve for m.**
m|b̄|² = −|ā|²
**m = −|ā|²/|b̄|²** ✓
**Check with concrete vectors.** Take ā = 3î and b̄ = 4ĵ, which are perpendicular ✓ Then
|ā|² = 9 and |b̄|² = 16, so the formula gives m = **−9/16**.
Testing: ā + b̄ = (3, 4) and ā + mb̄ = (3, −9/4), and their dot product is
3(3) + 4(−9/4) = 9 − 9 = **0** ✓ perpendicular, as required.
**Why m must be negative.** Both |ā|² and |b̄|² are **positive**, so the quotient carries
the minus sign through ✓ That immediately rules out option (2), m = 1 — and indeed with
m = 1 the second vector would be ā + b̄ itself, which cannot be perpendicular to itself
unless it is the zero vector.
**Why m = −1 is not generally right.** Option (1) would be correct only in the special
case |ā| = |b̄|. The question states no such condition, so the answer must depend on both
magnitudes ✓ (It is a useful check, though: when the two vectors have equal length,
m = −1 and the condition becomes (ā + b̄) ⊥ (ā − b̄) — the familiar fact that the diagonals
of a **rhombus** are perpendicular.)
**The geometric reading.** ā + b̄ is one diagonal of the rectangle on ā and b̄. The vector
ā + mb̄ perpendicular to it must lean back against b̄ by just enough to cancel the
projection — and the amount, |ā|²/|b̄|², is precisely the ratio of the two squared sides ✓
∴ −|ā|²/|b̄|².

kcet|Mathematics|2013|42||0|0.s:
Simplify the denominator first — it turns out to be **identical** to the numerator.
**Step 1 — expand (1 − i)².**
(1 − i)² = 1 − 2i + i²
= 1 − 2i − 1
= **−2i**
(worth memorising alongside (1 + i)² = 2i.)
**Step 2 — simplify the denominator.**
1 − (1 − i)² = 1 − (−2i) = **1 + 2i**
**Step 3 — form the quotient.**
(1 + 2i)/(1 + 2i) = **1**
numerator and denominator being the same non-zero complex number.
**Step 4 — read off the modulus and amplitude of 1.**
**modulus** = |1| = **1**
**amplitude** = arg(1) = **0**, since 1 lies on the **positive real axis** ✓
so the answer is **1 and 0** ✓
**Confirming the division the long way.** Multiplying numerator and denominator by the
conjugate 1 − 2i:
numerator: (1 + 2i)(1 − 2i) = 1 + 4 = **5**
denominator: (1 + 2i)(1 − 2i) = **5**
quotient = 5/5 = **1** ✓
**Why the amplitude of a positive real is zero.** The argument measures the angle from the
positive real axis, and the point 1 lies **on** that axis ✓ (For −1 it would be π, for i
it would be π/2, and for −i it would be −π/2.)
**The shortcut the question rewards.** Once (1 − i)² is seen to be −2i, subtracting it
from 1 restores exactly the numerator, and any non-zero number divided by itself is **1**
— with no arithmetic at all ✓
**Reading the distractors.** Three of the four options have a **non-zero** amplitude,
which would place the number off the real axis. Since the quotient is exactly the real
number 1, only an amplitude of 0 is possible ✓ And option (1), √2 and π/6, has the wrong
modulus too.
∴ 1 and 0.

kcet|Mathematics|2014|13||0|0.s:
The matrix is **diagonal**, and the inverse of a diagonal matrix is found by
**reciprocating each diagonal entry** — no adjugate or determinant needed.
**Step 1 — note the form.** A = diag(**2, 3, 4**), with zeros everywhere off the diagonal.
**Step 2 — check it is invertible.** Its determinant is the product of the diagonal
entries:
|A| = 2 × 3 × 4 = **24 ≠ 0** ✓
**Step 3 — write the inverse.**
A⁻¹ = diag(**1/2, 1/3, 1/4**) ✓
**Check by multiplying.**
diag(2, 3, 4) × diag(1/2, 1/3, 1/4) = diag(2 × 1/2, 3 × 1/3, 4 × 1/4)
= diag(1, 1, 1) = **I** ✓
since the product of two diagonal matrices multiplies corresponding entries.
**Why the rule works.** A diagonal matrix scales each coordinate axis independently — the
first by 2, the second by 3, the third by 4. Undoing that means scaling each axis by the
**reciprocal** factor ✓ The axes never mix, which is why no off-diagonal entries appear.
**Reading the distractors.**
**diag(2, 3, 4)** ✗ — this is A itself, not its inverse.
**(1/24) diag(2, 3, 4)** ✗ — dividing by the determinant is right for the **adjugate**,
not for the matrix itself. Testing: (1/24)diag(2,3,4) × diag(2,3,4) = (1/24)diag(4, 9, 16)
= diag(1/6, 3/8, 2/3) ≠ I ✗
**(1/24) I** ✗ — the identity scaled, which multiplied by A gives (1/24)A ≠ I ✗
**The adjugate route, for comparison.** adj A = diag(12, 8, 6) — the products of the other
two diagonal entries — and dividing by |A| = 24 gives
diag(12/24, 8/24, 6/24) = diag(**1/2, 1/3, 1/4**) ✓ the same answer, with more work. For a
diagonal matrix the reciprocal rule is always quicker.
**A caution.** The rule needs **every** diagonal entry non-zero. A single zero on the
diagonal makes the determinant zero and the matrix singular, with no inverse at all ✓

Expand both determinants, differentiate Q, and the answer appears as a multiple of P.
**Step 1 — expand P.**
P = | x  1 ; 1  x | = x·x − 1·1 = **x² − 1**
**Step 2 — expand Q** along the first row.
Q = | x 1 1 ; 1 x 1 ; 1 1 x |
= x(x·x − 1·1) − 1(1·x − 1·1) + 1(1·1 − x·1)
= x(x² − 1) − (x − 1) + (1 − x)
= x³ − x − x + 1 + 1 − x
= **x³ − 3x + 2**
**Step 3 — differentiate Q.**
dQ/dx = 3x² − 3
= **3(x² − 1)**
**Step 4 — recognise P.** Since P = x² − 1,
**dQ/dx = 3P** ✓
**Check at a value.** At x = 2:
P = 4 − 1 = **3**
Q = 8 − 6 + 2 = **4**
dQ/dx = 3(4) − 3 = **9**, and 3P = 3(3) = **9** ✓
At x = 0: P = **−1**, dQ/dx = −3, and 3P = **−3** ✓
**Why the relationship is so clean.** Q factorises as
x³ − 3x + 2 = (x − 1)²(x + 2)
and P = (x − 1)(x + 1). Differentiating Q gives 3(x − 1)(x + 1) = 3P ✓ The repeated root
at x = 1 in Q is what makes its derivative share the factor (x − 1) with P.
**A structural reason.** Both determinants have the form "x on the diagonal, 1 elsewhere",
and differentiating such a determinant means summing the determinants obtained by
differentiating **one row at a time**. Each of Q's three rows contributes a 2 × 2 minor
equal to P, giving **3P** ✓ — which generalises: the n × n version differentiates to n
times the (n − 1) × (n − 1) version.
**Reading the distractors.** **3P + 1** and **1 − 3P** ✗ have a stray constant;
differentiating a polynomial with no linear-in-P remainder cannot produce one. **−3P** ✗
has the wrong sign: at x = 2, dQ/dx = 9 is **positive** while −3P = −9 ✗
∴ 3P.

Row operations reveal that two rows become **identical**, which forces the determinant to
vanish.
**Step 1 — write the determinant.**
| log x    log y    log z  |
| log 2x   log 2y   log 2z |
| log 3x   log 3y   log 3z |
**Step 2 — expand the entries using log(ab) = log a + log b.**
log 2x = **log 2 + log x**, and similarly throughout.
**Step 3 — apply the row operations R₂ → R₂ − R₁ and R₃ → R₃ − R₁**, which leave the
determinant unchanged:
R₂ − R₁ = (log 2, log 2, log 2)
R₃ − R₁ = (log 3, log 3, log 3)
so the determinant becomes
| log x   log y   log z |
| log 2   log 2   log 2 |
| log 3   log 3   log 3 |
**Step 4 — spot the proportional rows.** The second row is log 2 times (1, 1, 1) and the
third is log 3 times (1, 1, 1) — they are **proportional** to each other ✓ A determinant
with two proportional rows is **0**:
**the value is 0** ✓
**An even quicker route.** Take log 2 out of the second row and log 3 out of the third:
log2 × log3 × | log x  log y  log z ; 1  1  1 ; 1  1  1 |
and the last two rows are now **identical**, so the determinant is **0** ✓
**Check with numbers.** Take x = 10, y = 100, z = 1000 with logarithms to base 10, so
log x = 1, log y = 2, log z = 3 and log 2 = 0·3010, log 3 = 0·4771:
| 1      2      3     |
| 1·301  2·301  3·301 |
| 1·477  2·477  3·477 |
Subtracting the first row from each of the others gives two rows of constants — 0·301
repeated and 0·477 repeated ✓ and the determinant is **0** ✓
**Why the conditions are stated.** "x, y, z not equal and ≠ 0, ≠ 1" ensures the logarithms
are defined and that the first row is not itself degenerate — but the answer is **0**
regardless, since the vanishing comes from rows 2 and 3, not row 1 ✓ The conditions are
there to make the question well posed, not to affect the value.
**Reading the distractors.** **log(xyz)**, **log(6xyz)** and **log(x + y + z)** ✗ all
depend on x, y, z, yet the row operations show the determinant is **independent** of them
entirely. A determinant that reduces to two proportional rows can only be zero ✓
∴ 0.
